content.text:
**Letter A**, on both dimensions.

**Clarity — A.** A is easier for a non-financial reader to follow. It signposts ("Three items from the quarter are worth noting… First… Second… Third"), and it translates jargon instead of repeating it: "the extra yield these bonds offered over safer bonds had narrowed to its slimmest margin since 2021" is comprehensible, where B's "credit spreads have narrowed significantly" leaves the key term undefined. A also explains *why* the cash position matters ("so that those distributions can be made without selling equity or other risk assets"), parenthetically defines gross-of-fees, and states the time-weighted/before-payments basis so the reader knows what the 2.2% does and does not include. B's sequencing works against the reader: it refers to pre-funding "upcoming distributions" a full paragraph before it explains what the distribution is or how it's calculated, and its denser paragraphs bundle two unrelated portfolio moves into one block.

**Tone — A.** The tone notes are specific and A meets them: formal letterhead, date, trustee salutation to Mrs. Delacourt in her fiduciary capacity, account reference, full trust name, and a cc to Mr. Ambrose. B opens "Dear Mrs. Delacourt and Mr. Ambrose," which collapses the trustee/income-beneficiary distinction that the file draws deliberately, and it drops the letterhead, date, and cc line entirely. B also drifts toward retail-marketing register — "your portfolio," "We successfully executed our plan," "your continued trust in our partnership," and a closing pledge to "providing steady income and preserving capital for your future needs." For a nine-year formal relationship that phrasing reads as both over-familiar and faintly promissory; A's "Thank you, as always, for your continued confidence" is warmer in the right way and carries no forward-looking commitment. Neither letter betrays the internal retention concern, but B's closing sentence edges closest to sounding like a pitch.

**Overall — A**, and not because it is longer; it is comparable in length and simply better organized and better matched to the client.

input.reason: Clarity: A signposts its three commentary items explicitly, glosses jargon in plain English ("the extra yield these bonds offered over safer bonds" vs. B's unexplained "credit spreads"), states the measurement basis (time-weighted, before unitrust payments), and explains the purpose of the cash build. B refers to pre-funding "upcoming distributions" before it has explained the distribution at all, and packs two unrelated portfolio moves into one dense paragraph. Tone: the tone notes call for formality, addressing the trustee as Mrs. Delacourt, full trust name, and a cc to Mr. Ambrose. A delivers all of that plus letterhead, date, and account reference; B drops the letterhead, date, and cc, and jointly addresses trustee and income beneficiary, blurring the fiduciary distinction. B also slips into retail-marketing register ("your portfolio," "We successfully executed our plan," "your continued trust in our partnership," and a closing commitment to "providing steady income and preserving capital"), which is over-familiar for a nine-year formal relationship and faintly promissory. Neither letter leaks the internal retention concern. Lengths are comparable, so the preference is not a length effect.
